concepts.label: Electric current
concepts.subject: physics
concepts.definition: The rate at which electric charge flows past a point in a circuit, measured in amperes.

concepts.label: Potential difference
concepts.subject: physics
concepts.definition: The work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points, measured in volts.

concepts.label: Electrical resistance
concepts.subject: physics
concepts.definition: How strongly a conductor opposes the flow of current through it, measured in ohms.

concepts.label: Ohm's law
concepts.subject: physics
concepts.definition: For many conductors at constant temperature the current is proportional to the potential difference across them.

sources.title: Mock reference notes, electricity (written for testing the knowledge base)

passages.text: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit. It equals the charge that passes divided by the time taken, and its unit is the ampere.
By convention the direction of current is taken from the positive terminal of the cell to the negative terminal. The electrons that carry the charge in a metal wire actually move the opposite way.
Potential difference between two points is the work done to move one unit of charge from one point to the other. Its unit is the volt, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the two points.
Resistance measures how much a conductor opposes the flow of current through it. Its unit is the ohm. For a given potential difference, a larger resistance allows a smaller current.

Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided its temperature and other physical conditions stay the same. This gives V equals I times R, where R is a constant for that conductor.

Not every conductor obeys Ohm's law. A graph of potential difference against current is a straight line through the origin for an ohmic conductor, and is curved for a non-ohmic device such as a filament lamp whose temperature changes as current flows.
The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross section, and it depends on the material and the temperature.

A picture that helps is water in a pipe. The tank stands for the battery, the pipe for the wire and the running water for the current. The height of the tank is the push, and a narrow part of the pipe holds the flow back. Charges are not water and a wire is not a pipe, so the picture shows how the push and what holds it back decide the flow, and nothing more.

In a metal the moving charges collide with the atoms of the material, and every collision holds the flow back. A longer wire gives more collisions, and a thinner wire gives more collisions, so a longer or thinner wire has more resistance.

claims.statement: Electric current is the charge that passes a point in a circuit divided by the time taken.
The conventional direction of current is from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, and the electrons in a metal wire move the opposite way.
conditions: in a metal wire, where electrons carry the charge

claims.statement: Potential difference between two points is the work done to move one unit of charge from one point to the other.
A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the two points whose potential difference is measured.
Resistance measures how much a conductor opposes the flow of current, and for a given potential difference a larger resistance allows a smaller current.
The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross section.
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, so V equals I times R with R constant.
conditions: the temperature and other physical conditions stay the same

claims.statement: A graph of potential difference against current is a straight line through the origin for an ohmic conductor and is curved for a non-ohmic device such as a filament lamp.
A 4 ohm resistor with 12 volts across it carries a current of 3 amperes.
conditions: an ohmic resistor at constant temperature

claims.statement: Current is the flow of electrons.

simplification.limit: in electrolytes and semiconductors the charge carriers are ions or holes, and conventional current is defined opposite to electron flow

claims.statement: Water in a pipe is a picture of current in a wire: the tank stands for the battery, the pipe for the wire and the running water for the current, and the height of the tank is the push.

simplification.limit: charges are not water and a wire is not a pipe: the picture shows how the push and what holds it back decide the flow, and nothing about what a charge is

claims.statement: In a metal the moving charges collide with the atoms of the material and every collision holds the flow back, so a longer or thinner wire has more resistance.

mistake.why: A larger resistance lets less current through, so the current cannot be found by multiplying the potential difference by the resistance.
